name: Coding Help That Teaches
title: Coding Help That Teaches
answer: Coding help that teaches means an AI tool should explain an error message and ask the student what they think is wrong, rather than supplying corrected code. This matters because AI can write working code quickly, which can let a program run and an assignment be finished while the student learns little. The aim is to keep the student doing the thinking.

sections.body: In computer science, AI creates a specific problem because it can produce working code in seconds. A student who is stuck can ask for the fix, paste it in, and see the program run without understanding the error. The idea of coding help that teaches is to make the tool support diagnosis and reasoning instead of replacing them. A tool set up this way explains what an error message means and asks the student what they believe is wrong. It does not write the corrected code for them.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: For schools, the principle points toward configuring coding tools so they prompt and question rather than solve, and the text says tools used in schools should be set up this way wherever possible. Age rules shape how this happens. GitHub Copilot is available through its education program only to verified students 13 and older. Code.org is designed for all ages, and students under 13 use accounts set up by a teacher or school. For younger students, a teacher can demonstrate coding help on a shared screen instead of giving students direct access.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book describes the research on this as sobering, and in a university programming course students were split into three groups: one used a tutor that gave hints, one used a chatbot that could give full solutions, and one used no AI. Both AI groups scored higher on the exercise, but neither learned more than the group without AI (Bassner et al., 2026). The students preferred the chatbot that helped them least. A review of generative AI in computer science education also flagged the risk of AI errors and invented information in code help (Adejumo et al., 2026). Those studies involved university students, and similar research in schools has not yet been found.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets limits around both tool behavior and student access. AI code help can produce errors and invented information, so it cannot be treated as a reliable authority. The decision about how a tool is configured stays with the school, and the text says school tools should explain errors and ask students what they think is wrong rather than write corrected code. Age rules also stay with adults: GitHub Copilot's education program is only for verified students 13 and older, and Code.org accounts for students under 13 are set up by a teacher or school. For younger students, the teacher can demonstrate coding help on a shared screen rather than give direct access.
